tldr: A benchmark that compares VLA fine-tuning, imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and LLM coding agents under identical conditions, faithfully reproducing the gait sway and control delays of a whole-body controller (WBC).
hero_caption: Initial and completed states across all 20 household tasks in BiGym 2.0. Covering reaching, tabletop manipulation, dishwashers, and kitchen counters, the suite features diverse scenes with locomotion and delicate contact.
overview:
For humanoid robots to work in household environments, loco-manipulation—moving the arms accurately while walking and maintaining balance—is essential. However, existing benchmarks often assume an idealized planar base (floating base) like a wheeled mobile robot. As a result, they fail to adequately evaluate how real physical behaviors such as footstep impacts, torso sway, and control delays affect manipulation.

To address this, the authors built BiGym 2.0, redesigning household tasks for the Unitree G1. Integrating a balance and locomotion controller (GR00T-WBC), they collected high-quality human demonstration data via VR executed through this whole-body controller (60 episodes per task, 1,200 episodes total).

What makes this study especially compelling is that alongside VLA (Vision-Language-Action model) fine-tuning, imitation learning (ACT, Diffusion Policy), and demonstration-driven reinforcement learning (RL), it directly compares control programs autonomously written by LLM coding agents (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5) under the exact same observation and action interfaces.

Experimental results show that the VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$ achieved the highest mean success rate across nine representative tasks. However, on bimanual target reaching, coding agents that constructed independent feedback loops for each arm outperformed all learned policies. Meanwhile, long-horizon tasks combining locomotion and delicate grasping—such as multi-object transport and cross-workspace block stacking—remain open challenges for all approaches.
contributions: Designed 20 household tasks for the Unitree G1 and open-sourced 1,200 high-quality human VR demonstrations collected natively through a unified whole-body controller (WBC).
Rigorously evaluated VLA fine-tuning, imitation learning, and offline/online demo-driven RL under deterministic resets that restore the internal state of the whole-body controller.
Audited the capabilities and failure modes of LLM coding agents generating code policies from a cold start using the same low-resolution onboard camera views and joint command interfaces.
Empirically identified specific physical challenges unique to bipedal loco-manipulation, such as grasp slip caused by footstep impacts and tracking difficulties from moving viewpoints.

sections.heading: Battling Footstep Sway: A New Challenge for Humanoid Manipulation Benchmarks
sections.summary: Unlike wheeled platforms, a bipedal humanoid experiences footstep impacts and torso sway that directly interfere with arm manipulation. This work provides the first head-to-head comparison between data-driven learned policies and LLM agent code synthesis under a rigorous, realistic whole-body control environment.
sections.details:
Household humanoids are expected to seamlessly bridge walking and bimanual manipulation, whether loading a dishwasher or carrying objects across a room. Robot capability development has largely evolved along two distinct paths: data-driven approaches like VLAs and imitation learning, and agentic approaches where LLMs assemble environment APIs into executable code.

Yet, no prior work has benchmarked them on the exact same physical execution stack. While wheeled mobile bases can smoothly follow velocity commands, a legged robot's whole-body controller (WBC) operates through dynamic gaits, inevitably introducing control delays, vibrations, and torso tilt. These serve as significant physical disturbances directly affecting end-effector precision.

While the original BiGym offered 40 tasks for the Unitree H1, its demonstrations were collected in a floating-base mode that bypassed dynamic leg steps, decoupling locomotion dynamics from manipulation. In this work, the authors redesigned task geometries for the compact Unitree G1, gathered human VR demonstrations teleoperated directly through the WBC, and established BiGym 2.0 as a deterministic benchmark that restores controller internal states upon reset.

Furthermore, the authors introduced a cold-start audit for LLM coding agents. Given only the same low-resolution ($84\times 84$) onboard camera views and proprioception—without inverse kinematics (IK) tools—agents synthesized control code under identical budgets, revealing the strengths and shared frontiers of both paradigms.

sections.heading: Lineage of Manipulation Benchmarks and the Rise of Code-Synthesizing Policies
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes its contributions across manipulation benchmarks, whole-body teleoperation frameworks, humanoid learning suites, and LLM-based policy synthesis, highlighting the gap it uniquely bridges.
sections.details:
Humanoid control and benchmarking are advancing rapidly, and this work sits right at their intersection.

- Manipulation benchmarks: Suites like RLBench, LIBERO, and RoboCasa are prominent, but they center on stationary arms or wheeled bases. While the original BiGym pioneered household tasks on the H1, its base dynamics were simplified as noted above.
- Whole-body control (WBC) and teleoperation: Platforms such as ExBody, GR00T, and Open-TeleVision have emerged for full-body humanoid teleoperation. This paper uses a frozen GR00T-WBC across both demonstration collection and evaluation.
- Humanoid learning environments: HumanoidBench, SIMPLE, and HumanoidArena have recently appeared, but none combined native human demonstrations gathered through a WBC with a unified evaluation of learned policies and coding agents.
- Policy learning vs. code synthesis: On the learned side, OpenVLA, $\pi_{0.5}$, ACT, Diffusion Policy, and demo-driven RL compete closely. Meanwhile, code generation approaches starting from Code as Policies (CaP) to ASPIRE and RHO have LLMs write control scripts directly. This study audits code synthesis under a strict interaction step budget matched to online RL.

sections.heading: Designing an Environment Grounded in Realistic Physics and Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: BiGym 2.0 integrates 20 household tasks customized for the Unitree G1 with GR00T-WBC, provides 1,200 high-quality human VR demonstrations, and establishes an evaluation protocol guaranteeing bit-level reproducibility.
sections.details:
### III-A Loco-manipulation Challenges and Task Design
The environment is structured around two core physical challenges: contacts under gait disturbances and coordinated multi-object transport. The 20 tasks span four domains:
- Reaching (3 tasks): single-arm reach, multimodal target reaching with either arm, and dual-arm reach.
- Tabletop (5 tasks): moving plates, inverting cups and cutlery, and stacking blocks across tables.
- Dishwasher (4 tasks): closing the door, inserting cutlery, and loading cups and plates.
- Kitchen counter (8 tasks): opening/closing drawers and cabinets, lifting and carrying boxes, and moving pans.
Task geometry is tailored to the G1's workspace, and success criteria require holding target contacts or placements stably for 1 second.

### III-B Whole-Body Control Stack
The robot is a 29-DoF Unitree G1 equipped with Dex1 hands. Policies output arm joint position targets, gripper commands, and base velocity/yaw/height commands at 50 Hz. The frozen GR00T-WBC ingests these setpoints and coordinates the 12 leg joints and 3 torso joints at a 1 ms simulation step to maintain balance.

### III-C Human Demonstration Collection
Using a Meta Quest 3 VR headset and Mink inverse kinematics, operators provided real-time arm targets and base locomotion commands. Because the WBC mediates execution during data collection, the demonstrations naturally contain gait lag and body sway. A total of 1,200 successful demonstrations were recorded (60 per task across 20 tasks).

### III-D Observations and Deterministic Resets
Policies receive three onboard camera feeds (head and wrist cameras at $84\times 84$ RGB) and 50–56 dimensional proprioception (joint positions, velocities, etc.). Crucially, the authors enforce reset determinism: because the WBC maintains internal state, merely fixing the simulation seed leads to diverging trajectories. BiGym 2.0 restores the WBC's internal state snapshot, ensuring bit-for-bit trajectory replay.

### III-E Policy Baselines
The benchmark evaluates $\pi_{0.5}$ (VLA fine-tuning), ACT and Diffusion Policy (DP) for imitation learning, and demo-driven RL baselines including online CQN-AS, DrQ-v2+, and offline DEAS. Furthermore, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were deployed as cold-start coding agents within the interaction budget of online RL (101k steps).

sections.heading: Learned Policies vs. Coding Agents: Where Each Paradigm Excels and Falters
sections.summary: Benchmarking across nine representative tasks revealed that the VLA ($\pi_{0.5}$) led the overall average. However, coding agents decisively outperformed learned models on bimanual reaching, while multi-object transport remained difficult across the board.
sections.details:
### IV-A Dual Reaching vs. Transport Tasks
Kinematically constrained, stereotyped motions like drawer closing saw high success rates across nearly all methods. However, bimanual reaching highlighted a stark divergence between paradigms. Learned policies that performed well on single-arm reach saw performance drop sharply when required to coordinate both arms simultaneously. In contrast, coding agents (Astra and Opus) wrote parallel, independent feedback loops for each arm, outperforming every learned policy.

Conversely, on contact-rich transport tasks such as moving plates or inserting cups, $\pi_{0.5}$ demonstrated solid performance, whereas coding agents struggled to complete them. Interestingly, Opus achieved high success on pick-box, a task where $\pi_{0.5}$ struggled, showing that VLAs do not dominate universally.

### IV-B The Pitfall of Best-Checkpoint Selection
In imitation learning, papers frequently report peak performance from the single best checkpoint. To guard against optimistic bias from overfitting evaluation seeds, this study adopts the mean of the final five checkpoints (Last-5 mean) as its primary metric. Relying solely on peak checkpoints artificially inflated scores by up to 13 points, making this strict protocol vital for fair comparison.

### IV-C Broadening the Task Suite
Across the remaining 11 tasks, ACT and CQN-AS achieved over 10% success on several environments. However, cross-workspace block stacking (stack_blocks)—requiring the robot to walk between tables while assembling a three-block tower—remained unsolved, with imitation learning and RL scoring under 1%.

sections.heading: Inside the Coding Agents: How They Reason and Why Physical Contact Trips Them Up
sections.summary: Even under strict observation constraints, LLM agents managed to synthesize visual servoing and memory-reconstructed kinematics models. However, when faced with extended transport and delicate contact states, limited trial budgets led to persistent failure.
sections.details:
### V-A Agent Harness and Interfaces
Agents (GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5) ran inside isolated Docker containers, restricted from external internet access except for their model APIs.
Remarkably, although the strict interface provided no IK solver, Claude Opus 5.5 reconstructed the Unitree G1's kinematic link dimensions (URDF parameters) from pre-training memory and implemented a custom numerical IK solver using SciPy in 24 out of 27 sessions. GPT-6 Astra took the opposite route: without building a geometric model, it wrote pure visual-servoing loops tracking pixel errors from wrist cameras. Despite completely different approaches, their final nine-task mean scores were virtually identical.

### V-B Fragility in Contact-Rich Dynamics
While agent-synthesized code navigated free space reliably, it frequently failed during plate manipulation and cup insertion, where delicate contact dynamics govern success. High inter-session variance was also observed: an agent might devise a perfect strategy in one session, but produce code that completely stalled in another.

### V-C Benefits of Robotics Tools and the Block-Stacking Barrier
When supplied with high-resolution imagery, camera calibrations, and a differential IK solver in an augmented tool interface, Astra improved substantially on cupboard opening and cup insertion. Yet on the hardest challenge, block stacking, its success peaked at 19%. With an interaction budget of 101,000 steps, a long-horizon task requiring up to 8,750 steps per attempt permitted only about 11 rollouts—too few for the agent to debug code and refine control strategies.

sections.heading: Cold-Start Assumptions and the Caveats of Simulation Benchmarks
sections.summary: The agent evaluation represents a performance floor due to its task-isolated 'cold-start' setup without skill accumulation. Furthermore, reliance on a single simulation environment and frozen controller presents important limitations.
sections.details:
The coding agents in this benchmark operated strictly from a cold start, developing solutions from a blank slate for every task. While this ensures an apples-to-apples comparison with policies trained on individual tasks, equipping agents with skill libraries that accumulate and reuse code assets across tasks could unlock much higher performance.

Additionally, all evaluations were conducted in simulation using a single controller stack, GR00T-WBC. When a policy commands a base velocity, how that command translates into joint torques and foot-ground interaction depends heavily on WBC tuning. Furthermore, because Claude remembered G1 link parameters from its pre-training data, agent behavior may differ when applied to less documented or proprietary robot morphologies.

sections.heading: Setting a New Bar for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation: Fusing Data and Code
sections.summary: BiGym 2.0 establishes a rigorous benchmark for humanoid household tasks that incorporates dynamic walking and whole-body control. It maps out the distinct strengths of VLAs and coding agents alongside the open challenges that remain.
sections.details:
BiGym 2.0 demonstrates where current state-of-the-art policy paradigms stand when confronted with the real physical disturbances of bipedal walking and torso motion. While VLA fine-tuning ($\pi_{0.5}$) posted the highest overall mean success rate and handled delicate transport tasks well, LLM coding agents proved superior at bimanual reaching by explicitly programming decoupled arm feedback loops.

Nevertheless, multi-object handling across work areas and precise block stacking remain unsolved across all tested methods. By open-sourcing the simulation suite, human demonstrations, and full evaluation traces, the authors provide a solid foundation for future research into skill-accumulating agents and diverse whole-body controllers.

sections.heading: Appendix: Demonstration Kinematics, Controller Determinism, and Foot-Ground Contacts
sections.summary: The appendix details kinematic statistics across the 1,200 human demonstrations, contact parameter adjustments that eliminate gait-induced grasp slip, and mechanisms for camera placement and evaluation reproducibility.
sections.details:
### Mitigating Grasp Slip from Footstep Impacts (F-A)
In realistic simulation, footstep impacts (peaking around 3.45 Hz) propagated through the torso into the arms, causing plates held in the gripper to slip and rotate over time. The authors found this was caused by inadequate torsional friction in the Dex1 finger pad model. Raising torsional friction from 0.01 to 0.05 and tuning contact damping reduced slip from 0.745 mm down to 0.002 mm over a 6-second carry, enabling stable grasps without artificial weld constraints.

### Why DrQ-v2+ Diverged (F-B)
The online RL baseline DrQ-v2+ scored 0% on most tasks. Log analysis revealed that the robot repeatedly drifted backward or sideways out of the workspace (drifting an average of 4.2 m) until timing out. This failure highlights the difficulty of single-step control without action chunking under dynamic base behaviors.

### Kinematic Statistics of Human Demonstrations (Appendix C)
The 1,200 VR demonstrations span durations from 2.9 s to 87.4 s (median 14.4 s) and base travel distances from 0.06 m for stationary manipulation up to 8.10 m for transport tasks. Peak pelvis tilt reached 6.4° to 27.9° across all episodes due to stepping and reaching, confirming that the demonstrations incorporate substantial posture dynamics.

takeaways: When evaluating humanoid loco-manipulation, floating-base approximations must be discarded in favor of realistic whole-body controllers that capture gait vibration and control latency.

While imitation learning and VLAs experience sharp performance drops when scaling from single-arm to bimanual coordination, coding agents exhibit superior robustness by synthesizing explicit parallel feedback loops for each arm.
Frontier LLMs like Claude Opus 5.5 can recall robot URDF link parameters from pre-training memory to construct working numerical IK solvers entirely from scratch without dedicated tools.
Ensuring reproducible simulation rollouts requires restoring the internal state of the whole-body controller alongside the simulator random seed.
limitations: The coding agent audit is restricted to a task-isolated 'cold-start' setup, meaning performance improvements from accumulating and reusing code libraries across tasks were not evaluated.

Evaluations are limited to simulation using a single whole-body controller (GR00T-WBC) and platform (Unitree G1); generalizability across alternative controllers or physical hardware dynamics remains untested.
Because LLM agents recalled G1 URDF specifications from pre-training data, it is unclear whether they can achieve similar code synthesis performance on novel or poorly documented robot platforms.
